_doc: T-3645: every evidence note a building's Details tab shows as its "Why" (tools/reading_notes.mjs), retold for younger readers. Keyed by the note's own words, since many claims share a note. Only the younger ages are written; no fact enters that the note does not hold, and the build's own talk (record ids, kit names, pixel and camera readings) is left out, so a young reader gets what was read and from where, and what is a guess.

8-10: The map writes "1" inside the building. So it has one floor.

The map writes "2" on the barn and "1" on the low part. The barn is built with a room for carriages at the bottom and a loft above. The low part has one floor and a flat roof. How tall they are is our guess. The map shows no roof window, so none is built.
The map writes "2" on the building. It is built with a room for carriages and a loft above. The roof slopes up from there to a flat top. There is no floor in the roof.

The map writes "2" on the building, so it has two floors. It has a room for carriages, with a loft above, under a sloped roof. How tall they are is our guess. The map draws no roof window, so none is built.
The map writes "2" on the building, so it has two floors. It has a room for carriages, with a loft above. How tall they are is our guess.

The map writes "2" on the stable and "1" on the small part by the yard. So they have two floors and one. The stable has a room for carriages, with a loft above, under a sloped roof. How tall they are is our guess. The map draws no roof window, so none is built.
The map writes "2" on the stable, so it has two floors. It writes "1" on the long low part and on the small part by the yard, so each has one floor. How tall they are is our guess.
The map writes "2" on the stable, so it has two floors. It writes "1" on the long low part, so it has one floor. How tall it is is our guess.
The map writes "2" on each part, so it has two floors all the way through.
The 1911 map writes "2" on this part. The photo shows two full floors over a raised floor. The porch is about six steps above the yard.
The 1911 map prints "2" over the east building, with the word GARAGE. The long low parts have one floor.

"2B" is written in one corner on the map. That means two floors over a basement. The bottom is a room for carriages. Above it is a loft. How tall they are is our guess. The basement is under the ground, so it is not built.
The map prints "2BB" on the house. So it has two floors and a basement.
The 1911 map prints "2BB." That means two full floors. The photo shows them over a raised basement. The porch floor and the front door are about 1.55 meters above the sidewalk.
The 1911 map prints "2BB." That means two full floors. The "BB" does not mean two basements. The house stands on a low base, over a cellar we do not know about.
The 1911 map prints "2½ and 3B; rear1B." So it has 2 full floors and a half floor in the roof.

The map writes "2½," two and a half floors. The bottom is a room for carriages, with a loft above. The half floor is under the roof. How tall they are is our guess. The map shows no roof window, so none is built.
The 1911 map prints "2½B." That means two full floors of brick, and a half floor in the roof. The map gives a wall thickness for only two floors. So the half floor is the attic, lit by a roof window.

The 1911 map prints "2½B; rear3B." That means two full floors over a raised basement, and a half floor. The photo shows the half floor as a short third floor across the front, under the trim. A steep roof rises above it. An 1883 book of pictures agrees. The brick back parts have three floors.

The 1911 map says "2½S.B." That means two full floors over a raised basement, and a half floor. In 1869 the Tribune newspaper said the attic was lit by small windows in the top trim. So it is built as a short third floor, with its windows in the trim. The photo shows them on the south side.
The 1911 map prints "2½S.B." over the front part. Two old pictures show it too. It had two full floors of brick over a raised basement. It had a half floor up in the roof too, lit by roof windows.

The 1911 map says this house had two full floors and a basement. It had a half floor up in the roof too. The photo shows two floors of brick on a stone basement. You can see the basement windows above the fence.
The 1911 map says "3B brick with stone front." A check of old records calls this house a brownstone front.
The 1911 map calls it a stone house with three floors and a basement. The photo shows cut stone on the front on Prairie Avenue. It shows the same stone on the side on 18th Street.
The 1911 map prints "3B." That means three full floors over a basement.
The 1911 map prints "3B." That means three full floors over a basement.
The 1911 map prints "3B" over the front part. An 1895 picture shows three floors over a raised basement.
The 1911 map prints "3B." That means 3 full floors. The photo shows them over a raised basement. A note from 1884 calls it a house with three floors.
The 1911 map prints "3B." That means three full floors over a basement.
The 1911 map says "3B," three floors and a basement. A picture from 1891 shows three floors over a low basement.

The 1911 map prints "3BB" over the front part. That means three floors over a raised basement. The north part is marked "2," and a room at the back of the south side is marked "2BB." They are built with those floors. The parts with no mark get three floors, like the house.

The 1911 map prints "3BB" over the front part. That means three floors over a raised basement. The north part is marked "2," and the back part on the south side "1." They are built with those floors. The parts with no mark get three floors, like the house.

The 1911 map says "3½B." That means three floors over a basement, and a half floor in the roof. A photo from 1890 agrees. It shows three floors of windows, and an attic with three windows in the pointed front.
The basement windows were all above the ground, a paper said. They are in the stone under the main windows.
The main floor is 1.4 meters above the ground, like the house next door. The map does not show the basement. It fits a whole number of steps up the front.
The roof slopes at 45 degrees, the steepest we build. In the old drawing the roof rises to about 12.7 meters. A roof this steep reaches that height.
This is our guess. A brick side wall 13 inches thick, our usual wall. No record tells how thick it was.
A brick wall 13 inches thick, like the house it is joined to. The map gives no wall thickness for this lot.
A brick wall 13 inches thick. The map gives no wall thickness for this lot.
This is our guess. Trim with brackets along the street, under the edge of the flat roof. No record shows it.
This is our guess. Wood trim with brackets along the street, under the edge of the flat roof. No record shows it.
Wood trim with brackets along the street, under the flat roof's top edge. It runs on across the shared wall, as one trim over both houses. No record shows it.

Next to the south bay there is a blank row with no window. Then comes the door's row, and one row of windows north of it. The old print shows these two rows on the sunny side of the front. The south bay is south of the door.
Trim with brackets runs around the walls under the roof. The photo shows pairs of brackets under a deep top, along the front and the south side.

Trim with brackets under the mansard roof. The photo shows a dark band of brackets across the front. How they looked up close is not known, so we build our usual wood trim with brackets on all four walls.
This is our guess. How thick a brick front on a fireproof frame was. No record measures it.
This is our guess. How thick the brick front is, on a stone basement. No record measures it.
This is our guess. How thick the brick front is, over a stone basement. No picture shows it clearly.
This is our guess. A brick wall with a stone face, 18 inches thick, like another stone front. The map's blue band shows the front's stone. It does not show how thick it was.
A group of bronze figures that George M. Pullman paid for. It was put near his house in 1893. People thought the battle of 15 August 1812 was fought near there.
A deep roof edge, in an Italian style. In the photo the top trim sticks far out, about 0.75 meters. The corner is at a slant in the photo, so this is our guess.
Deep trim on small blocks, at the top of the second floor, under the mansard roof. One old photo shows it. It is built as our usual stone trim.
Heavy stone trim runs under the roof, around the front and along the 20th Street side. The photo shows it over the north bay and the corner.
A heavy stone trim across the whole front, over a band carved with flowers. Its top is about 14.2 meters up. It is built as our stone trim. The small blocks and the carved flowers are not built.

A low roof that slopes on all sides, behind the roof edge with brackets. The first plan had attic windows too. No record shows this roof. But a low roof was the most common on brick houses on this street then.
A landing before the door. The photo sees the steps from the end, so how deep it was is not known.
A low wall along the sidewalk, like the house next door. In the photo the yard is covered with building stone. In the other picture a tree hides the fence.

A low roof that slopes on all sides, behind the trim with brackets. One roof covers the front house and its two-floor back wing. The map draws them as one brick building. The photo shows no roof over the trim and no roof windows.
A low roof that slopes on all sides, behind the top trim. It has a flat top with a railing. The photo shows the railing.
A mansard roof. Both pictures draw its steep slate sides with roof windows over the trim, on the front and the north side.
A mansard roof. The drawing shows its steep slate sides with roof windows, over the trim. The map's "3B" counts it as the third floor.
A mansard roof. In the photo the roof rises in steep slate sides over the trim, with roof windows in them. At the top is a flat part with an iron railing.
There is stone trim at the top of the wall. The old print shows the roof start from a band of stone there.
In the photo there is stone trim at the top of the wall, under the slate. It runs around the corner and the top of the tower.
The steps are narrow. The door is in a small flat strip of front, 1.37 meters wide, between the round bay and the north corner.
The steps are narrow. The door is in a small flat strip of front, about 2 meters wide, between the round bay and the south corner.
A plain roof edge over the north wall. The photo shows a small trim there. How deep it was is not known.

This is our guess. The main floor is raised over a basement. The map draws a stone porch at the door, at the top of the steps. The plan asks for tall steps. It fits a whole number of steps up the front.
This is our guess. The main floor is raised over the basement the map's "B" tells of. It is like two other houses on the street. It fits a whole number of steps up the front.
This is our guess. A front of rough stone blocks on a brick back. No record tells how thick it was.
A front of rough stone, with brick behind it. It is the thickest kind of stone front we build.
A short landing at the door, about 1.5 meters. Then the steps turn down to the path. The photo shows it.

The photo shows a slate roof sloping down to the street, across the whole front. So the roof slopes to the front and the back. It is closed at the sides by the shared walls. It has a roof window on the street side, and a pointed cone roof on the round tower. No picture sees the back of the roof.
A mansard roof of slate over the front, with a roof window with a pointed top. The north part has its own steep roof. The photo taken straight on shows them.
A mansard roof of slate, with roof windows, in the photo. The museum says it was added in the 1880s.
A mansard roof of slate, with roof windows over the front and the south side. Both photos show it.
A mansard roof of slate, with roof windows over the front. One old photo shows it.

A smooth, light stone front, as the 1883 picture and the old print show. It is built in Bedford limestone. Its base is two rows of stone deep, under a main floor 2.35 meters up. Which stone it really was is our guess. The pictures only say it was light and smooth.
A stone front on a brick back, like all our stone fronts.
This is our guess. How thick the stone front is, as thick as we can make it. In the photo the windows sit deep, but it can't be measured.
This is our guess. How thick the stone front is. No picture shows it clearly.
This is our guess. How thick the stone front is. No picture shows it clearly.

A stone front on the street, with brick side walls. A picture from 1883 draws the front light and smooth, next to a darker brick side wall. Another old print draws a stone base and stone corners on the front, against brick on the side. The 1911 map colors the building brick, which is the main body. We were told not to make every wall stone, so only the street front is stone.
A stone wall on the street, 18 inches thick, for a house with three floors. It is like our other stone fronts.

In the photo and an 1883 picture, a very steep slate roof rises from the trim. It has a short flat top with an iron edge, over the north corner. Our mansard roof with straight steep sides is that roof.
About the frame around the door.
The middle of the building's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 10.4 meters deep and 17.5 meters long along the alley. It is one box, with no parts added on.
The middle of the building's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 7.6 meters deep and 12 meters long along the alley.
The middle of the building's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 10.4 meters deep and 19.4 meters long along the alley.

The middle of the building's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 4.5 meters deep and 6.2 meters long along the alley. Its north wall is just south of the edge of the lot, where the next stable's south wall is.
The middle of the building's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 11.7 meters deep and 14.1 meters long along the alley.
The middle of the building's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 13.9 meters deep and 7 meters long along the alley.
The middle of the building's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 10.5 meters deep and 11 meters long along the alley.
The middle of the building's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 11.9 meters deep and 8 meters long along the alley.

The middle of the building's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 7.4 meters deep and 16.3 meters long along the alley. It fills the whole back of the lot. An 1886 map shows a long building here too.

The middle of the building's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 15.3 meters deep and 7.7 meters long along the alley. It fills the whole width of the lot, up to 18th Street.

The middle of the building's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 14 meters deep and 15.2 meters long along the alley. A dashed line on the map crosses inside it. It is not built.
The middle of the building's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map, from the alley back to its east wall. It is 9.15 meters deep.

The middle of the building's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 10.6 meters deep and 17.6 meters long along the alley. Its north wall is shared with the next lot's building. South of it is an open strip about 3 meters wide.
The middle of the building's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 10.7 meters deep and 22.4 meters long along the alley. That is almost the whole width of the lot.

The middle of the building's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 14.6 meters deep and 8.5 meters long along the alley. That is the lot's whole width. Both ends stand against the buildings next door.
The middle of the shed's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 9.2 meters deep and 3.9 meters long along the alley. Its south wall is shared with the next lot's stable.

The middle of the stable's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 7.5 meters deep and 16.3 meters long along the alley. Its north wall is shared with the next lot's building.

The middle of the barn's wall on the alley. The 1911 map draws the barn from the alley back to its east wall. It is 9.07 meters deep. The low part next to it is just as deep, so one depth is built for both.
The middle of the stable's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 7.8 meters deep and 9.8 meters long along the alley.

The middle of the stable's wall on the alley. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 10.1 meters deep and 16.6 meters long along the alley. A long low part runs on south from the stable, 4.2 meters deep, to the edge of the lot.

The middle of the building's west wall. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. It is 9.5 meters along the west wall. Its east wall runs along the slanted line of the train tracks. So it is about 15.6 meters deep on the north side, and 18.4 on the south.

The middle of the palm house, a glass room for palm trees. Its size was measured from the 1911 map. The long wing runs from the house's east wall to the small tower. It is about 4.4 meters deep. A round room is in it, with a terrace in front and wide steps.

An all-stone house. Both photos show the same light cut stone on the front and the south side. The 1911 map colors the house stone. The map's brick back part, which no picture shows, is built as a brick back wing.
The side walls of an all-stone house are as thick as its front. The photo shows the side in the same cut stone.
A small basement window in the front wall. The map's "B" says there was a basement.
There is a small window for the basement under each front window. The "B" on the map says there was a basement.
An iron fence on a stone base just inside the street line, with stone posts at the path. The picture shows it in front of the house and the houses next door.
This is our guess. Small windows for the basement in the front wall, under the main floor.
Small windows for the basement in the front wall. They are under the main floor. The "B" on the map says there was a basement.
There are small windows for the basement in the front wall. They are under the raised main floor. The map does not print a B for a basement.
Small basement windows in the front wall. The map's "B" says there was a basement.
Small basement windows in the front wall. The map's "B" says there was a basement. But on this front the wood bay and the steps stand where they would go, so none is cut.
These are small basement windows, north of the bay. The bay has its own pair, with bars, above them.
Small basement windows under the main windows, 0.65 meters tall. They fit under two rough rows of stone and the cap.
Small basement windows under the main windows. The two under the round bay are the old drawing's own.
There are small windows for the basement. They are under the two front windows. The "B" on the map says there was a basement.
This is the same as the front. Each outside wall has the same brick over the same stone base. A paper from 1869 said so.
There are small windows for the basement. There is one under each main window, about as wide as the one above. Both photos show them behind the fence.
Basement windows under the main ones, in the old photo, and under the bay, in the photo with the car. Their tops are at the top of the stone base.
Basement windows under the main ones, about 1 meter wide. The photo with the car shows them. They are built a bit shorter, so their tops meet the top of the stone base.
The map colors both parts pink, its color for brick. Numbers on the walls give how thick they were, in inches. Our walls are built a bit thicker, our usual size.
Both photos show a mansard roof of slate over the top trim. It has roof windows with pointed tops, and a flat top with a railing.

Both photos show round arches over the main floor's street windows, with a small center stone at the top. The top of each arch is a carved panel over a square window. It is built as round glass, and its dark color looks like the shadow of the carving.
Both side walls are shared with the houses next door. The 1911 map draws them joined, and no window shows in either.

Brownstone, a brown stone, smooth, over two rough rows at the bottom. The map says only stone. A newspaper of 1890 called the house "the brown stone mansion No. 1634." We have not checked that paper ourselves, so the color is still our guess.

Brownstone, a brown stone, smooth, over two rough rows at the bottom. It is the same stone as the house it is paired with. The map draws the two fronts as one pair in one stone. A newspaper of 1890 called the other house "the brown stone mansion." Nothing tells about this house's own stone, so it is our guess.
It was built from 1 June 1886 to 1 December 1887. That was the night the family first slept in it.

In one photo, the upper window on the north is about 9.2 meters along. That is half a meter past the door, which is under the porch in another picture. So the upper floor's windows are spaced on their own.
Plain brick, a 13-inch wall. The map gives no wall thickness for this lot.
Plain brick, a 13-inch wall. The map gives no wall thickness.
Copper gutters behind the top trim, and two pipes at the back. The newspaper tells of copper trim. No picture shows them.
The photo's front and side are smooth cut stone in rows, with deeper rows at the bottom. A list of buildings calls it brownstone. The photo is black and white, so it can't show the color.
Windows that slide up and down, getting smaller going up. They match the house it is joined to.
This is our guess. Windows that slide up and down, getting smaller going up. They are like another house on the street. No record shows them.
The windows slide up and down. They get smaller on each floor going up. That is like another house on the street.
Windows that slide up and down. They get smaller on each floor going up.
Windows that slide up and down. They get smaller going up. They match the house it is joined to, so the windows line up across the shared wall.
Windows that slide up and down. They get smaller going up. There are three floors, with a lower fourth under the top trim.
Windows that slide up and down, getting smaller going up. They are like another house on the street. The third floor's windows are a little lower, so they fit under the trim at the top.
The map colors the stable and the long low part pink, its color for brick. Numbers on the walls give how thick they were, in inches. An 1886 map colors them pink too, for brick.
The map colors all the parts pink, its color for brick. Numbers on the walls give how thick they were, in inches. An 1886 map colors them pink too, for brick.
The map colors it pink, its color for brick. Numbers on the walls give how thick they were, in inches. A mark on the north wall shows a fire wall. An 1886 map colors it pink too, for brick.
The map colors it pink, its color for brick. Numbers on the walls give how thick they were, in inches. An 1886 map colors it pink too, for brick.

The 1911 map colors it pink, its color for brick. Numbers on the north and south walls give how thick the walls were, 12 inches at the bottom and 8 above. A mark at the end of each wall shows a wall built to stop fires. An 1886 map colors it pink too, for brick.
The 1911 map colors it pink, its color for brick. Numbers on the walls give how thick they were, in inches. An 1886 map shows a wood building here. Only the 1911 map shows it as brick.

The map colors it pink, its color for brick. Numbers on its north and south walls, 12 and 8, give how thick they were, in inches.
The map colors it pink, its color for brick. Numbers on its north wall, 12 and 8, give how thick the walls were, in inches.
The 1911 map colors it pink, its color for brick. The numbers on one wall, 12 and 8, are how thick the walls were, in inches. Our walls are built a little thicker, our usual size.
The map colors it yellow, its color for wood. So it has thin wood walls, never thick stone or brick ones.
The map colors it yellow, its color for wood. So it is built board by board, with thin wood walls, never thick stone or brick ones.
The map colors it yellow, its color for wood. So it is built board by board, with thin wood walls.
The map colors it yellow, its color for wood. The photo shows the front in long wood boards, with boards at the corners. It is built board by board, with thin wood walls.
Every street window, on both floors, has a stone top with a little roof on brackets. Both photos show them. The carving on the brackets is our guess.

Every wall the old pictures show is the same dark red brick, on the front and the long north side. So red-brown brick is used all around. A photo from 2004, after the house was fixed up, shows red brick on both sides.
Every window is two panes over two, like the house it is joined to. That is not from this house. The basement windows are our usual small ones.
Every window has two panes on top and two below. The old drawing shows one bar across the middle of each window. It also shows curtains pulled back.
Every window is two panes over two, our most common kind. That is not from this house. The basement windows are our usual small ones.
Each window has two panes on top and two below. The basement has our usual small windows.

Five windows on each floor along the south wall, in two groups, with the down pipe between. The wall is long, so it could hold more. But a deep row house lit its middle rooms from its open side. The north wall is blank.
Windows and doors with flat tops on both floors. The photo taken straight on shows them.

In the photo, the north corner has openings with flat tops under stone caps. That is the door and the window over it. The attic window has a plain top. The south part's pair of round-topped windows is its own kind.
Windows with flat tops, under stone caps, on both floors of the new front's bay. The photo with the car shows them.
Windows with flat tops, under small stone caps, on both floors. Two old photos show them.
The height of each floor, getting lower going up. They match the house it is joined to, so the floors, sills and trim line up across the shared wall. No record gives this house's heights.
This is our guess. Each floor is a bit lower than the one below it. That is like two other houses on the street with flat roofs. The top of the wall is 12.3 meters up.
Each floor is a bit lower than the one below it. That is like another house on the street with three floors. The first plan was a little different. No record gives this house's heights.

The height of each floor. These were measured from the photo, at the south corner of the front. The upper window sills are 5.5 meters above the main floor. The top of the wall is about 12 meters above the ground.
The height of each floor matches the house it is paired with. That way the floors, top trim and low top walls line up across the shared wall. The top of the wall is 12.3 meters up.

The height of each floor. The main floor and the second are each 3.9 meters. That was worked out from the old drawing. The top of the wall is set at 9.2 meters, so the round bay can rise under the top trim. No sizes are written on the drawing.

The height of each floor. The main floor is 3.9 meters, so the second floor lands at the bottom of the bay window. The second floor is 4 meters, so the top of the wall is at 9.75 meters, at the top trim in the drawing. No sizes are written on the drawing.
The height of each floor. The main floor is 4.3 meters and the second is 4.9. They were worked out from the old drawing. The top trim is about 11.5 meters up. No sizes are written on the drawing.

The height of each floor. The main floor is the tallest, like the house next door. They were made taller than the first plan, so the windows and roof edge fit under a low roof. No record gives this house's heights.

The floors were worked out from the windows in the photo. The second floor is about 6.2 meters up. The side walls stop at about 10.6 meters. These are tall floors for a row house, as the pictures show next to the house next door.
Four rows across the 9.58 meter front, measured from the photo. The door is in the second row. The second floor's windows are right over the ones below.
Both photos show four rows of windows on each house.
Four windows on each floor along the south wall. The side yard next door is about 3.6 meters wide.

The size of this part of the greenhouse, measured from the 1911 map. It is 12.59 meters long and 8.34 meters wide. The map draws a dashed line with a gap at its south end. That is the door into the next part.

The size of this part of the greenhouse, measured from the 1911 map. It is 23.71 meters long and 8.9 meters wide. Its north end meets the room at the top. Its south end is the gate house's north wall.
The size of this part of the greenhouse, measured from the 1911 map. It is 16.84 meters long and 7.13 meters wide. Its west end is the gate house's east wall. Its east end meets the round end.
The size of this part of the greenhouse, measured from the 1911 map. It is 2.93 meters long and 5.51 meters wide. Its straight part runs to the middle of the half circle drawn at the east end.
Glass on a light frame. The old picture shows a ring of tall windows and a glass roof with ribs. The map writes "Greenhouse" on the bulge.
Mr. Glessner and a study from 1963 say the stone is granite from Wellesley. The museum says it is pink granite from Braggville. No one knows which is right, so the card does not name it.
He bought the land in March 1885. He kept the house until December 1924. Then he gave it to a group of architects in Chicago.
How far the top trim sticks out. It matches the house it is joined to, so the trim runs on as one.
How far the top trim sticks out, under the low wall at the top. It is like the house a few doors down.
The sides and back are built in brick. The 1911 map colors the house stone, and a photo shows a rough stone south side. So the brick stands in for it. It is light yellow, for the light stone.
The side and back walls are plain brick, as the 1911 map colors them. In the photo the north side looks paler than the front. The photo is black and white, so the light yellow brick is our guess.
This is our guess. A copper gutter and two pipes, out of sight from the street. No picture shows them.
This is our guess. A copper gutter behind the top trim, and two pipes. No picture shows them.

The round bay. Its place and size come from the 1911 map. It sticks out about a meter from the front and is 3.76 meters across. Everything else is our guess. It goes up all four floors, from the ground to the stone trim at the top. It has three windows on each floor. It is stone, like the front.
The photo shows a tall stone chimney with panels, rising off the north side behind the corner part. A second one is on the south side, where the map draws it. No picture shows that one.
The terrace and the porch floor are at the top of the steps. They are about 2.2 meters up. In the photo there are about eleven steps. We measured all the other heights from this one.

The terrace and porch floor at the top of the front steps. The 1898 picture shows about thirteen steps between the side walls. That is about 2.4 meters high. The old print shows the terrace at the same height.
The outline puts the curved bay on the north half of the front, at the 16th Street corner. So the door is on the south half.

The upper floors' window sills and glass were measured from the Christmas picture. The sills are 5.74 and 9.19 meters up. No picture shows the main floor's windows. Their sizes, and all the widths, are our guess.
The porch floor that the steps go up to. On the 1911 map the wood porch stands 1.8 meters in front of the house. It runs the whole width of the house.
The little picture shows deep trim across the top of the front, with brackets. The other drawing shows the brackets in pairs. It is built as our trim with brackets, like the house next door.
In the little picture, the steps go up under the porch's columns.
In the little picture, each window has a top that sticks out, like a small roof. The other drawing shows one over every window on both floors. So both floors get our stone top with a little roof.

The main floor is about 4.9 meters tall, and the second about 4.7 meters. That was worked out from the old photo, by the size of the windows and the door. The new front of 1880 was built to the old floors. The roof edge is about 11.6 meters up, a bit lower than the house next door.
This is our guess. A path of flat stones from the bottom of the steps to the gate. A path of cinders goes to the back, for workers.
The path to the steps is made of flat stones, like the other houses on the street.

Both old pictures show the whole front in rough stone blocks, in rows. The sills and bands are smooth stone. The pictures are black and white. The stone looks pale, lighter than the brick next door. So it is built as a pale limestone. The kind of stone and its color are our guess.
Our usual yard, as on the block's other fine houses.

Three rows across the 6.55 meter front. The door and the windows over it are at one end. Then come two windows on each floor. Three rows was the usual width for a narrow row house. No record shows it.

Three rows across the 6.55 meter front. First come two windows on each floor, next to the shared wall. Then the door and the windows over it, at the south end. It is the mirror of the house it is joined to.
Three rows across the 6.75 meter front, worked out from the photo's three upper windows. The main floor's two windows and the door are under them, behind the porch.

Three rows across the 7.6 meter front, worked out from the photo. The north part has two windows on each floor. In the photo the second floor's windows are a bit south of the ones below. We cannot build that, so they line up. The door is in the middle of the fancy frame, with one window on each floor above it.

Three rows across the 8 meter front. Two are behind the wood bay, which has its own windows on the two lower floors. So those two rows have windows only on the third floor. On the north is the door, with a window on each floor above it.
The walls are 14.7 meters tall. The 1911 map prints 48 feet to the roof edge. A church does not have floors like a house. We use three tall floors only to set the wall height and the rows of windows.

The walls are 14.7 meters tall to the roof edge, as a picture from 1901 shows. A church does not have floors like a house. We use three tall floors only to set the wall height and the rows of windows.

This is our guess. Three plain brick chimneys. Two are on the south wall, and one is on the north wall. They are over the walls between the rooms of a long house. No record shows this house's chimneys.

Three boxes, measured from old drawings of the church. One is the main hall. One is the hall for meetings, with the rooms by the front of the church. One is the north side part. The entry rooms and the side supports are part of the boxes.
Three rows of windows across the front, where the drawing puts them. First the door's row, then the one next to it, then the one on the part that sticks out.

Three windows on each floor along the south wall, over the side path. There is one for each room, in a house three rooms deep. One window is behind the wood part that sticks out, so it is not cut. That part has its own window. No record shows them.
Three windows on each floor along the north wall, one for each room. They match the side windows of the house it is paired with. The wall faces the side yard next door.
Three windows on each floor along the south wall. The path to the house next door is about a meter wide. How many there are, and where, is our guess.
Three windows on each floor along the south wall. They stay clear of the part that sticks out and its down pipe.
Three windows on each floor in the house's north side wall, over the narrow path next door. There is one for each room, in a house three rooms deep. No picture shows this wall.
Measured from the photo. The second floor is about 6.6 meters up. The top of the trim is about 12 meters up. A deep band is over the second floor's windows.
Measured from the photo. The middle bay's second floor window is from about 7.8 to 10.5 meters up. The main floor's windows are hidden behind ivy, so they are built tall.

Measured from the photo. The main windows are about 0.95 meters wide. They go from about 3 meters up to about 5.25 meters, at the top of the arch. The upper windows are about 0.9 meters wide. They go from about 6.85 meters to about 9 meters.
Worked out from the picture. The door is about 1.4 meters from the north corner. The ground floor's two windows are at 4 and 5.8 meters.

Two bays from the 1911 map. A slanted bay is on the south side. It is in the front's stone, two floors high, as both photos show. A box sticks out on the north side, 7.4 meters long. No picture shows its windows, so they are our guess.

Two rows across the 6.2 meter front. First is the door, in the strip north of the bay, with a window over it on each floor. Then comes the middle of the round bay. The old drawing and the 1911 map do not agree on the sizes. The map wins, as it did for the house next door.
Two rows across the 6.75 meter front. On the south side is the slanted bay, with its own windows. On the north side are the door and the window over it.
Two rows across the 7 meter front. On the south side are the door and the window over it. On the north side is the curved bay, with its own windows.
Two rows across the 7.45 meter front. On the south is the door, with a window on each floor above it. On the north is the slanted bay, with its own windows.
Two rows across the 7.7 meter front. On the south is the slanted bay, with its own windows. On the north is the door, with a window on each floor above it.

Two rows across the 8.46 meter front. First is the door, in the middle of the strip north of the round bay, with a window over it on each floor. Then comes the middle of the round bay. The wall behind the bay is not cut.
Two rows along the front, from the north corner. First the door and the window over it. Then the round tower. The photo shows where they are.
Two rows along the front, from the north corner. First is the row of windows. Then comes the door. They were measured from the photo.
Two brick chimneys on the top of the roof, over the walls between the front and back rooms, like the house next door. No record tells about this house's chimneys.
Two brick chimneys on the top of the roof, over the walls between the front and back rooms. No record tells about this house's chimneys.
Two brick chimneys on the short top of the roof, over the walls between the front and back rooms, like the houses next door. No record tells about this house's chimneys.

The photo shows two chimney tops above the trim. So there are two brick chimneys with stone tops. One is over the south wall, about 4 meters back. One is over the north wall, about 3.3 meters back. The photo shows which way they are, but not how far back. So where they stand is our guess.

Two rows across the front. On the south is the middle of the slanted bay. On the north are the door and the window over it. The bay covers the front's windows behind it, on both floors, and has its own.
Two rows across the front. On the south are the door and the windows over it. On the north is the middle of the wood bay. The last bit on the north is a plain corner by the edge of the lot.

Two full floors, over a tall basement, with one more floor in the roof. The photo shows two rows of windows in the walls and a third row in the roof windows. A map from 1911 says "3S.B.," three floors of brick. It counts the roof floor as the third.
Two full floors over a raised basement, under a mansard roof, as the photo shows on both street sides. The map's "3B" counts the floor in the roof.

Two full floors over a raised basement, with a floor in the roof. The photo shows this on the front and the south side. The map says "3B," counting the roof floor as the third, as it does for other houses.

Two full floors over a raised basement, with a third floor up in the mansard roof. The 1911 map prints "3B." An 1893 drawing shows two rows of windows over the basement windows, under a mansard roof with roof windows. So the third floor is in the roof.
Two full floors over a raised basement, with a floor in the roof lit by roof windows. The old drawing shows this. The 1911 map prints "2½B," the same count, with a half floor in the roof.

Two rows of openings across the 7.5 meter front. One is over the north half of the slanted bay. The other is the door, with a window on each floor above it. The Christmas picture shows two windows on the third floor and one on the second, north of the bay. Where they sit was worked out from the picture.

Two plain brick chimneys come up through the roof, by the wall shared with the house next door. The other house has two of its own there. So the two roofs have pairs of chimneys side by side. That was common for houses built as a pair. No record shows this house's chimneys.
Two plain brick chimneys come up through the roof, by the wall shared with the house next door. That is like another house on the street. No record shows this house's chimneys.
Two plain brick chimneys come up through the roof, by the wall shared with the house next door. That is like another house on the street. No record shows this house's chimneys.
Two plain brick chimneys come up through the roof, on the south wall at the edge of the lot. They are over the walls between the front, middle and back rooms. No record shows this house's chimneys.
Two square windows in the basement, under the ground floor's two. Their tops are 1.33 meters up. They have iron bars.
This is our guess. Two chimneys in the side walls. The old picture does not show a chimney clearly.
This is our guess. Two chimneys on the side walls. Neither photo shows the chimneys.

Two floors of brick over a raised basement, under a mansard roof. A drawing from about 1914 shows the walls stop at trim over the second floor, with the steep roof above. A little picture from 1898 shows the second floor's windows under the trim. The 1911 map counts the attic in the roof as the third floor.

Two floors of brick over a raised stone basement, under a mansard roof. In the photo the walls stop at trim with brackets over the second floor. The roof's steep sides rise above it, with roof windows. The 1911 map says "3S.B." It counts the attic in the roof as the third floor.

Two floors of brick over a raised stone basement, under a mansard roof. In the old picture, the walls stop at trim with brackets over the second floor. The roof's steep slate sides rise above it, with roof windows. The 1911 map counts the attic in the roof as the third floor.

Two floors over a raised basement, in the old print and in a picture from 1898. The south bay goes up one more floor, like a tower. The 1911 map says "3B." We think it counts the basement, whose windows stand above the ground under the front terrace.

Two floors over a raised basement, with a floor in the mansard roof, as the photo shows. The 1911 map says "3B," counting the roof floor. The museum says the third floor roof was added in the 1880s. That was before 1904.

Two floors over a raised basement, under a mansard roof with an attic in it. A drawing from May 1874 shows two rows of windows under one top trim, with the mansard roof and its roof windows above. A Tribune drawing from 1898 shows two floors of windows too. Nothing we read says it changed by 1904. The 1911 map no longer shows the house.
The photo shows two tall stone chimneys with shaped tops, over the south side. Where they stand along the wall is our guess.
Two floors of walls over a raised basement, under a mansard roof with roof windows. Two old photos show it. The 1911 map's "3B" counts the roof as the third floor.
Two floors of walls over a raised basement, under a mansard roof. That was read off the photo taken straight on. The 1911 map's "3B" counts the roof as a floor.

Two floors of walls over a raised basement, under a mansard roof. An old photo with a car, from about 1897, shows the main floor and the bottom of the second. Another photo shows both floors and the roof. The 1911 map says "3B." It counts the floor in the roof.

Two floors over a raised basement. An old photo from before 1880 shows the house's two tall floors, with steps up to the main floor. A photo with a car, from about 1900, shows the new stone front's slanted bay, two floors high. The 1911 map's "2½B" counts a half floor. That is the attic behind the deep top trim.
Two windows on each floor along the north wall, over the side yard next door. A wall facing a yard gets windows, but fewer than the south side. This is our guess. The map shows no windows.
Two windows on each floor in the back wall. The one over the back wing is not cut on the floors the wing covers. The other looks into the open yard next to the wing.
Two windows on each floor in the back wall. The one over the back wing is not cut on the floors the wing covers. The other looks into the open yard next to the wing.
In the photo, each window has two sheets of glass with a bar between them.
Two panes over two, our usual window for a brick front of the time. The drawing's window bars can't be seen.
Under the main floor, with their tops on the cap of the stone base.
It can't be seen, behind the stone railing.

This was checked on 30 September 2026, on the museum's own history page. In 1946 the house was changed for a new owner, a printing group. The house was changed, but it was not torn down. The model shows it only as it was in 1904.
One book says it was put up in 1893, near Prairie Avenue and 18th Street. Another says Pullman paid for it in 1893. It was taken away in 1931.
Windows along the north side, from the back to the front. The drawing shows two of them, over the garden wall. The back one was moved in a little, to clear the corner.

The main part is 6.2 meters deep, from the 1911 map. Two wings with bays stick out on its south side. The 1886 map draws them stepped. Their size and spacing come from the old photo. How deep they are is our guess.
The 1911 map marks this house '2½B'. That means two full floors and a half floor in the roof. The half floor is the attic under the front's pointed roof. The photo shows its three windows.
The side wall is brick, 13 inches thick. That was the usual wall.
The front wall is brick, three bricks thick. That was the usual front.
A flat step stands in front of the porch door. That was the usual kind.

In the photo, a picket fence stands in the snow in front of the side wing. We do not know just where it ran or how tall it was. So a plain board fence about 4 feet tall stands there, with a gate between two posts. The fence at the front is a guess too.
There is no ledge along the top of the front. The front wall goes right up into its pointed roof. The sides end at a plain slate roof edge. The photo shows this.
No picture shows the back wall. So it has the usual windows.
The tops of the street windows are plain stone. In the photo they look like pale stripes. There is no carving over them.
The 1911 map colors the house brick. The photo shows brick walls from the bottom to the top of the pointed roof. The round tower is brick too.
The porch has a round arch. It is at the north end of the front, under the round tower.
The steps are the usual kind.

In the photo, the steps climb along the front from the north, under snow. They are as wide as the arch, about 6 feet. Here the steps come straight out from the door instead. That is not how the photo shows them.
No picture shows the north side of the front part. So it has two windows of the usual kind. The front one lines up with the window on the south side.

The 1911 map shows the outline of the main part of the house. It is 60 feet from front to back and 30 feet wide. The round corner at the north-west is the tower. The part that sticks out on the south side is the side wing. The map shows a small cut at the front's south corner, about 3 feet. It is left out, because the photo shows a square corner.
In the photo, the front, the tower and the south side are all the same dark brick. The photo is black and white. So the red color is a guess, like the other brick fronts on the street.

The photo shows one rain pipe. It runs down the south side from the roof to the ground, where the side wing starts. Here the pipes stand at the back corner of the side wall instead. That is about 33 feet back along the side, close enough.
The photo shows slate on every roof. That includes the tower's pointed cap. Snow lies on it.
In the photo, the slate roof hangs out over the south side by about a foot.

The house had a round tower on the north corner of the front, over the porch. A list of the street's houses says so. The tower starts at the second floor and goes up to the roof edge, about 32 feet up. A pointed slate cap tops it at about 47 feet. A small spike sat on the very top. It is left off. The 1911 map shows the tower about 9 feet wide. Here it is a half round, about 8 feet wide and 4 feet out from the wall.
A walk of flat stones leads to the steps, like the other houses on the street. In the photo the yard is under snow.

In 1869 the Tribune newspaper said the roof would be slate, with copper trim. But our slate can only go on steep roofs, and this roof is low. So it is built in painted tin, with copper trim. The slate is written down in our list of guesses. In 2026 the tin was painted black. Now it looks dark, like slate.
